doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Natural love of music and the one-hour practice limit
summary: Early memories of music, Soloff and Rubin calling him a natural, and neighbors' complaints limiting practice to an hour.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: They stayed where they were and you got better.
Well they might have still improved but I just — zoom, like “Star Wars.” Getting away from the enemy.
Was there an aha moment or an epiphany or something along the way that caused you do get better like that?

Not get better, but two things that I’m going to mention at this clinic I’m doing for mostly rock & rollers, a couple of jazzers, this Friday, a couple of days from now, in Northampton, that I had mentioned to you. I was asked to do a clinic. So I’m going to talk about “Spinning Wheel” and the importance of an arrangement to make good music. That’s a good question. I’m forgetting your question. Oh an aha moment. First of all, when I was a little kid I remember being in the crib, I’m the middle kid, and my mother used to play radio, and at three years old, if I remember correctly, I’d be touched by music I’d hear like a “Gone With the Wind” theme on the French horn [scats] you know. And I don’t know if I cried, I mean I was just a little kid, but music has always been there. And two guys from Blood, Sweat & Tears, Lew Soloff, who you’ll probably mention later, and Alan Rubin, who sat in with the band and played on “Spinning Wheel” when Chuck Winfield was out. He had a problem with his lip or his son was born or something, so Alan played on “Spinning Wheel.” But those two guys, somewhere during the time I was with Blood, Sweat & Tears, they said, “You’re a natural, Fred.” I don’t know that they knew my background but they said like, “No one made you practice.” I said, “That’s true.” You just had the love for music. Like one of them said my dad or mom made me practice or something. I don’t know that. I felt a little hurt that they were pushed. Because I didn’t have that from my parents you know. My mom used to say, “Are you still in there practicing?” Where I lived in the project I could only play an hour a day because the neighbors complained. And when we moved it was in the lease: your son can only play an hour a day.
Oh it was in the lease. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

Yeah, when we moved to another place. Because someone had complained. They got a complaint, I used to go to school with him, his son played clarinet better than me and influenced me a little bit. But he called me up one day, I’m like, you know, public school. You know, I don’t want to go into it. He said — my parents weren’t on the phone it was just me. And he says, “You know you’re not supposed to play more than an hour.” And it put the fear into me. So I had years of being afraid of playing. Even now I mean I have a house, but the lady downstairs is very sweet. She says, “Play all you want you sound great.” And she’s like two floors away from me. It’s just me and my wife. So I have total freedom now. But for years in other places you’d have to wait until they’d go out of the house for groceries, and after playing with Blood, Sweat & Tears and all this stuff — so I own my own house too so it wasn’t a problem, but a lot of times there’s been that kind of anxiety, that fear of not — being sensitive to other people, not having them bother me.

It reminds me there’s an anecdote about Bix Beiderbecke when he was living, near the end of his life, and he was playing in this house where he was staying and he thought he was bothering people and they go, “No, no, keep playing.”
